text: In the summer of 1772, three of Europe's most powerful monarchies agreed to divide
large parts of a neighboring state between themselves.
The Kingdom of Prussia, the Russian Empire, and the Habsburg monarchy were about to carry
out what became known as the First Partition of Poland.
It was one of the most significant territorial changes in 18th century Europe.
A state that had once been among the largest on the continent was losing vast areas of
Not through a single decisive battle, but through an agreement negotiated by its powerful neighbors.
But how had Poland-Lithuania become so vulnerable?
Why were its political institutions unable to prevent foreign interference?
And what motivated three monarchies, despite their own rivalries, to cooperate in dividing its lands?
To understand the events of 1772, we have to go back more than a century.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth had been created in 1569 through the Union of Lublin.
It united the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under a common elected monarch
and parliament. It covered an enormous territory, stretching across much of Central and Eastern
Europe. Its population included Poles, Lithuanians, Ruthenians, Jews, Germans, and many other
communities. Different languages, religions, and traditions existed within its borders.
The Commonwealth had a political system that was unusual for its time.
The king was elected by the nobility, and important decisions were made by the same,
the national parliament. The noble class enjoyed extensive political privileges.
These freedoms were considered essential to the Commonwealth's political identity,
but the system also contained serious weaknesses. One of the most controversial institutions was
the Liberum Vito. Under this principle, a single deputy could object to a parliamentary
decision and bring an entire session to an end. Originally intended to protect the political
rights of the nobility, the practice increasingly made effective government difficult. Parliamentary
sessions could be disrupted, reforms blocked, and political decisions delayed. Foreign powers
soon learned how to exploit these divisions. During the 18th century, the Commonwealth became
increasingly dependent on its neighbors. Russia in particular gained enormous influence over
Polish politics. Its armies and diplomats played an important role in determining the
country's political direction. After the death of King Augustus III in 1763,
the question of succession once again became a European power struggle. With Russian support,
Stanisław August Poniatowski was elected king in 1764. Poniatowski hoped to modernize the state.
He supported administrative, economic, and educational reforms, and wanted to strengthen
the authority of the central government. However, these ambitions threatened powerful interests at
home and abroad. Russia, under Empress Catherine II, wanted to preserve its influence over the
Commonwealth. Prussia, ruled by Frederick II, also had little interest in seeing a stronger
Polish-Lithuanian state emerge between its territories. In 1767, Russian pressure forced
the Polish parliament to accept political arrangements that protected the rights of
religious dissenters and maintained important elements of the existing political system.
The Russian ambassador, Nicholas Repnin, used intimidation and political pressure to influence
the proceedings. For many Polish nobles, this was an unacceptable violation of their country's
independence. In 1768, opponents of Russian interference formed the Confederation of Bar.
This movement was made up of nobles who claimed to defend the Catholic faith,
traditional liberties, and the independence of the Commonwealth. They took up arms against the
king and the Russian influence surrounding his government. The resulting conflict,
known as the War of the Bar Confederation, lasted until 1772. The fighting further
weakened the Commonwealth. Russian forces intervened repeatedly, while the conflict attracted the
attention of neighboring powers. At the same time, Russia was fighting the Ottoman Empire
in a major war that had begun in 1768. Russian victories threatened the balance of power in
southeastern Europe. Austria, ruled by Maria Theresa, became increasingly concerned about
Russian expansion and its possible consequences for Habsburg interests. This created an opportunity
for Frederick II of Prussia. Frederick wanted to prevent Austria and Russia from becoming
involved in a wider conflict. He also sought a territorial connection between Brandenburg and his
eastern territories in Prussia. Rather than allow the rivalry between the great powers to develop
into a European war, he promoted a solution that would come at the expense of the Polish-Lithuanian
Commonwealth. The idea of partitioning Poland-Lithuania had become a practical political project.
In 1772, the three powers reached an agreement. Russia, Prussia, and Austria would each take
large portions of Commonwealth territory. Their armies moved into the areas they intended to annex,
establishing control before the Polish government could effectively resist. On the 5th of August,
1772, representatives of the three monarchies signed the partition treaty. The first partition
of Poland-Lithuania had become a reality. Each power gained different territories. Prussia
received royal Prussia, with the important exceptions of the cities of Danzig and Thorne,
which remained outside its control. It also gained territories in northern Greater Poland.
These acquisitions were particularly important to Frederick II. They strengthened the connection
between Brandenburg and East Prussia and gave Prussia greater control over important trade
routes along the Baltic coast and the Lower Vistula. Russia acquired extensive territories
in the northeast, including areas of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the eastern Commonwealth.
Although Russia received the largest geographical share, its main objective was also political,
maintaining its dominant influence over the remaining Polish-Lithuanian state.
Austria took territories in the south, including large parts of the region that would become
known as Galicia. For the Habsburg monarchy, these lands offered strategic advantages,
additional resources, and a stronger position in central Europe. The partition was not simply a
division of land. It was an attempt by three monarchies to reshape the balance of power in
Europe. The Commonwealth lost almost one third of its territory and approximately one third of its
population, yet it did not disappear. The Polish king, Stanisław August Poniatowski,
and the remaining government were confronted with a decision they had little power to influence.
The partitioning powers demanded that the same formally approve their territorial acquisitions.
In 1773, a special parliamentary session was convened under heavy pressure from the occupying
powers. Some deputies resisted. One of the most famous acts of protest came from Tadeuszuretan,
who attempted to prevent the proceedings from continuing. But resistance could not stop the
process. On the 30th of September 1773, the same ratified the partition treaties.
The loss of territory had now been given formal parliamentary approval.
For the people living in the annexed regions, the consequences were immediate. They found
themselves under new rulers, new administrations, and new legal systems. Taxes, military obligations,
and government institutions changed. Communities that had previously belonged to one political
state were now separated by new borders. In Prussian territories, German administrative
structures were introduced, and the monarchy strengthened its control over the newly acquired
lands. In the Austrian territories, the Habsburg government established its own provincial
administration. In the Russian acquisitions, the imperial authorities extended their influence
over lands that had previously belonged to the commonwealth. But the first partition did not
bring stability to the region. The remaining commonwealth still existed, and many of its
political leaders recognized that fundamental reforms were necessary if the state was to survive.
The experience of 1772 became a warning. A country divided by internal political conflicts and
weakened by foreign interference could lose its independence piece by piece.
In the following decades, reformers attempted to rebuild the commonwealth. Their efforts would
eventually lead to the constitution of the 3rd of May in 1791, one of the most important
constitutional reforms in European history. But the neighboring powers would not accept
the emergence of a stronger Polish-Lithuanian state. Further partitions would follow in 1793
and 1795. The first partition of 1772 was therefore not the end of Poland-Lithuania.
It was the beginning of the final struggle for its survival.
